title: The Trinity (CCC 253–256)
hookLine: one God in three persons, a communion of love

lines: WHO DID GOD LOVE BEFORE ANYTHING?
cards: A question a kid might ask at dinner: if God is love, who did God love before there was anything? Before the world, before angels, before people. Love needs someone to love, doesn't it?
You can't be love alone in an empty room. It sounds like a riddle. For Catholics, the answer is the central mystery of the faith, the one they name every time they make the sign of the cross.

teach.b: First, the words. Catholics believe in one God in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Jesus sends his apostles out, in the Douay-Rheims, "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." In the name, singular: one name, three persons. Second, what it isn't.

teach.h: NOT THREE GODS, NOT THREE MASKS.
teach.b: The Catechism, paragraphs 253 to 256, is careful: not three gods, and not one God wearing three masks.
Each person is fully God, and the three are really distinct from one another, distinct only in how they relate: the Father begets, the Son is begotten, the Spirit proceeds.
Early councils, at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381, fought hard for that language, and nearly every Christian church still professes it in the Creed. Third, the answer to the riddle.
If God is love, then from all eternity there is lover, beloved, and the love between them; Augustine put it almost that way sixteen centuries ago. God was never alone in an empty room.
God is a communion of self-giving love, before anything else existed, and creation, and each person, is invited in. Fourth, it's a mystery.
The Catechism calls the Trinity the central mystery of Christian faith, something no one could have figured out, only received.
A well-known story says Saint Patrick used a three-leafed shamrock to explain it; it's a story people tell, not something in his own writings, and every picture falls short.
The Church's answer: this is who God is, and it's love all the way down.

how: Catholics begin and end prayer with the sign of the cross in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, pray the Glory Be after each decade of the rosary, and keep Trinity Sunday the week after Pentecost.

o: one God who wears three masks at different times
three separate gods who work together as one
one God in three persons, Father, Son and Spirit

games.q: one God, three persons — tap the pairs.

s: one God in three persons, each fully God, really distinct in how they relate.
Saint Patrick's shamrock lesson comes from his own writings
it's a story people tell, from much later.
Jesus sends the apostles to baptize in the name, singular, of Father, Son and Spirit

games.q: a child asks: if God is love, who did God love before there was anything? what's the Catholic answer?
o: the Father, Son and Spirit loved one another from all eternity
God only became love after creation
games.why: Catholics say God is a communion of love from all eternity: lover, beloved and love, as Augustine put it.

practice: Pray, or hear, the Glory Be, one of the oldest and shortest Catholic prayers, breathing between each phrase: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.

As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen. If you pray, say it once more, slowly, and sit in the quiet after; if you don't, just listen to its shape: three names, one glory, always.

wordCard.voice: The Trinity. One God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit: the central mystery of Catholic faith, a communion of love. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: threeness, a word the early Latin writer Tertullian was among the first to use for God.

carryVoice: Your line: love is a communion. A shared laugh, a meal, a hand held: real togetherness is a small echo of what Catholics say God is. Day two hundred ninety-seven, done.
